editor_spans.body: The most concrete item in the Motherwell speech was not regional R&D money but an offer of DWP devolution: a localised employment-support model shaped by Holyrood. That is a real transfer of power from Westminster to Edinburgh, which is exactly the parliament-to-parliament swap the Prime Minister said deep devolution was not about.

The offer comes with a condition. The new system must follow the 'Easterhouse principle' and go 'right down', or in his words 'it won't work'. Westminster is offering Holyrood a power on the understanding that Holyrood will pass it on to its regions. That is a bargain, not a gift, and it puts the First Minister in the awkward position of turning down powers if he resists the strings.

The pressure is framed as competition. Scottish towns, he warned, risk being 'underpowered' while northern English cities 'power up'. The National Economic Council meeting with the devolved first ministers will set the stage. Using English mayoralties as the benchmark turns devolution inside Scotland into a contest Holyrood is invited to lose in public.

The reindustrialisation tools he named are telling. They are £10 million matched for two defence technical colleges, a defence sector of 12,000 Scottish jobs, shipbuilding, Grangemouth, and procurement that pays 'a little more' to buy British. The pattern is industry revived by the state as customer, increasingly a defence customer.

That is the honest lesson of Ravenscraig. Steel did not leave because places lacked a say. It left because nobody would pay for it once markets moved on. Bringing industry back means accepting higher costs, which the Prime Minister admits when he talks about choosing Falkirk-built buses. It also links his domestic agenda to the munitions shortfall exposed by Ukraine. Rearmament may become the main way Britain reindustrialises.
